sections.title: Emphasis with no and none
sections.content:
We can use no and none (of) instead of not a or not any for particular emphasis. Compare:
• There isn't a train until tomorrow. and There's no train until tomorrow. (more emphatic)
• Sorry, there isn't any left. and Sorry, there's none left.
• He didn't have any of the usual symptoms. and He had none of the usual symptoms.
We use other pairs of negative words and phrases in a similar way:
• There isn't anyone / anybody here. and There's no one / nobody here. (more emphatic)
• She wasn't anywhere to be seen. and She was nowhere to be seen.
• Why don't you ever call me? and Why do you never call me?

sections.title: Initial position
sections.content:
We don't usually use not a / any, not anyone, etc. to begin a sentence or clause, or straight after and, but or that. Instead we use no, none of, no one, etc.:
• No force was needed to make them move. (not Not any force was needed ...)
• Most players are under 16 and none of them is over 20. (not ... and not any of them ...)
• I'm sure that nothing can go wrong. (not ... that not anything can ...)

sections.title: Not a in formal style
sections.content:
In a formal or literary style we can use not a in initial position or after and, but or that:
• Not a sound came from the room. (less formally There wasn't a sound from the room.)
• She kept so quiet that not a soul in the house knew she was there.

sections.title: Singular or plural noun after no
sections.content:
After no, we can often use either a singular or a plural noun with little difference in meaning, although a singular noun is usually more formal:
• No answers could be found. (or more formally No answer ...)
• We want to go to the island but there are no boats to take us. (or more formally ... there is no boat.)
However, we use a singular noun in situations where we would expect one of something, and a plural noun where we would expect more than one. Compare:
• I phoned Sarah at home, but there was no answer. (not ... but there were no answers.)
• He seems very lonely at school, and has no friends. (not ... no friend.)

sections.title: Special emphasis
sections.content:
We can give special emphasis to no or none of using phrases like no amount of with uncountable nouns, not one ... / not a single ... with singular countable nouns, and not one of ... with plural nouns:
• The company is so badly managed that no amount of investment will make it successful.
• Not one person remembered my birthday. (or Not a single person ...)
• Not one of the families affected by the noise wants to move.
Whatsoever can also be added after a negative phrase to add emphasis:
• I have no interest whatsoever in taking up running.

sections.title: Informal spoken phrases with no
sections.content:
Some phrases with no are commonly used in informal spoken English:
- No wonder (= it's not surprising)
- No idea (= I don't know)
- No comment (= I have nothing to say)
- No way, No chance (= emphatic ways of saying 'no', particularly to express refusal to do or believe something)
- No problem, No bother (= it isn't / wasn't difficult to do something)
• 'The computer's not working again.' 'No wonder. It's not plugged in!'
• 'Thanks for the lift.' 'No problem. I had to go past the station anyway.'

exercises.question: Where are the biscuits? There are ___ in the cupboard.
exercises.hint: Use 'none' as a pronoun when it stands alone without a noun.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: none
Use 'none' as a pronoun when it stands alone without a noun.

exercises.sentence: There are no any seats left in the economy section of the flight.
exercises.correction: There are no seats left in the economy section of the flight.
exercises.hint: 'No' and 'any' are both negatives — never combine them.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: There are no seats left
'No' and 'not any' are equivalent and interchangeable — you cannot combine them. Choose one: 'There are NO seats left' (no + noun) OR 'There AREN'T ANY seats left' (not + any). 'No any' is never correct in standard English.

exercises.question: I've got a headache. - ___ . You've been in front of that computer screen for hours.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: No wonder
'No wonder' is a fixed expression meaning 'it is not surprising'. It is used as a reaction to an explanation: 'You've been working all day — no wonder you're tired.'

exercises.sentence: None of the solutions that were proposed were entirely satisfactory.
exercises.correction: None of the solutions that were proposed were entirely satisfactory.
acceptable: None of the solutions that were proposed were entirely satisfactory.
None of the solutions that were proposed was entirely satisfactory.
exercises.hint: 'None of' can take singular or plural verb — both are correct in modern English.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: were/was entirely satisfactory — BOTH CORRECT
'None of + plural noun' can take either a singular or plural verb in modern English. Historically, 'none' required singular ('none was'), but plural ('none were') is now widely accepted, especially in informal contexts. Both are grammatically valid; singular is slightly more formal.
exercises.prompt: Is this sentence correct? If not, rewrite it correctly.

exercises.question: I phoned the car hire company and had to wait hours for someone to turn up. It was hot and there (was no shade) as there (is no tree) in that part of the island. (Find the mistake in the phrase in brackets)
options: is no tree -> are no trees
was no shade -> wasn't any shade
is no tree -> was no trees
exercises.hint: Use a plural noun ('trees') where we would expect more than one.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is no tree -> are no trees
Use a plural noun ('trees') where we would expect more than one.

exercises.question: ___ of what she said at the meeting made any sense to us at all.
exercises.hint: 'None of + uncountable/singular noun' refers to zero amount.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: None of what she said
'None of' is used for zero quantity and can precede countable plural nouns ('none of the students') or uncountable/singular nouns ('none of the money', 'none of what she said'). 'No' (without 'of') is used directly before nouns: 'no money', 'no students'.

exercises.question: A: 'Can you give me a lift to the station?' B: '___ . I'll pick you up at eight.'
exercises.hint: 'No problem' means it isn't difficult to do.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: No problem
'No problem' means it isn't difficult to do.

exercises.question: I made lots of cakes for the party but ___ the children liked them. (Use an emphatic phrase)
exercises.hint: Use 'not one of' with plural nouns for special emphasis.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: not one of
Use 'not one of' with plural nouns for special emphasis.
